concept.name: CDN Architecture & Geo-Distributed Edge Caching

relationships.description: CDNs terminate client TCP/TLS connections physically close to users via Anycast to eliminate round-trip latency.
A CDN is essentially a globally distributed edge reverse proxy fleet with caching and DDoS mitigation.
Complements in-memory database caching (Redis) by filtering traffic before it reaches origin servers.

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Canonical masterclass systems architecture authored with BGP Anycast mechanics, Cache-Control header breakdown, and Fastly/Wikipedia case study.

spark.summary: A Content Delivery Network (CDN) terminates TCP/TLS and serves cached responses from Anycast edge PoPs milliseconds from the user, collapsing cross-continental RTTs and shielding origin servers from 80–99% of read traffic.
spark.keyTakeaway: Edge caching is won or lost in HTTP cache headers and collapse controls: combine `s-maxage`, `stale-while-revalidate`, Origin Shielding, and request coalescing so a single cache miss never becomes a 10,000-RPS origin stampede.

concept.whyItMatters: The speed of light in fiber (~200,000 km/s) imposes a hard ~150 ms round-trip floor between Bengaluru and Virginia. Because a standard TLS 1.2 + TCP handshake takes 3 RTTs before the first byte of HTTP data arrives, serving assets directly from a single origin adds 450+ ms of pure network tax. By terminating TLS 1.3 and HTTP/3 (QUIC) at an edge PoP 10 ms away and absorbing 95%+ of static and semi-dynamic reads, a CDN cuts tail latency by an order of magnitude and reduces origin egress bills by 70–90%.
whenToUse: Serving static assets (JS/CSS bundles, images, fonts, HLS/DASH video segments) globally with sub-50 ms TTFB.
Offloading high-read, low-mutation APIs (product catalogs, public profiles, news feeds, feature flags) using `Cache-Control: s-maxage` and `stale-while-revalidate`.
Protecting origins against volumetric L3/L4/L7 DDoS attacks and flash-sale traffic spikes via Anycast absorption and edge WAF/rate limiting.
whenNotToUse: Strongly consistent, user-mutated endpoints (account balances, shopping cart writes, checkout mutations) where stale reads cause financial or data-integrity bugs.
Private, uncacheable 1:1 WebSocket/gRPC streams with bespoke per-user payloads where edge caching adds zero hit ratio (though edge TLS termination and Argo/smart routing can still help).
Internal-only microservices communicating inside the same VPC/AZ where 0.5 ms east-west network hops make an external CDN hop counterproductive.
keyPoints: BGP Anycast routes users to the topologically closest healthy edge PoP using a single shared IP; if a PoP fails, BGP withdraws the route and traffic shifts seamlessly within seconds.

Separating `max-age` (browser cache) from `s-maxage` (CDN shared cache) lets you cache aggressively at the edge (e.g., 24 hours) with instant surrogate-key purging while keeping browser TTLs short (60 seconds).
`stale-while-revalidate` serves slightly expired content immediately (0 ms wait) while asynchronously refreshing from origin in the background, eliminating user-facing cache-miss latency spikes.

Origin Shielding (a tiered mid-gress cache layer between 300+ edge PoPs and your origin) collapses 300 regional misses into 1 origin fetch, preventing origin overload during cold starts or global purges.

Cache-key hygiene is everything: uncontrolled `Vary` headers (e.g., `Vary: User-Agent`) or unstripped marketing query parameters (`?utm_source=...`, `?fbclid=...`) fragment the cache key and tank hit ratios below 20%.

examples.title: Global News & Media Portal with Surrogate Keys and SWR
examples.scenario: A high-traffic media site publishes breaking news updates every 2 minutes to 40M daily readers. Previously, `Cache-Control: max-age=60` caused thousands of simultaneous edge misses every minute across 250 Cloudflare/Fastly PoPs.
examples.outcome: Switching to `Cache-Control: public, max-age=30, s-maxage=86400, stale-while-revalidate=120` paired with `Surrogate-Key: article-9821 homepage` headers lifted edge cache hit ratio from 71% to 98.4%. When an editor updates an article, a webhook issues a targeted surrogate-key purge in <150 ms globally, cutting origin RPS by 92%.

examples.title: Tiered Origin Shielding for Live Sports HLS Streaming
examples.scenario: During a live cricket match, 2.5M concurrent viewers request 2-second `.ts`/`.m4s` video segments across 180 edge PoPs, threatening to saturate the origin S3/media packager with 180x redundant fetches per segment.
examples.outcome: Enabling an Origin Shield PoP in Mumbai (`ap-south-1`) with request coalescing (collapsed forwarding) ensured that all 180 edge PoPs fetched each new 2-second segment from the shield, which made exactly 1 request to the origin packager—reducing origin egress from 1.8 Tbps to 10 Gbps.

tradeOffs.factor: Long Edge TTL + Active Purge vs. Short TTL
tradeOffs.pro: Long `s-maxage` (hours/days) with `Surrogate-Key` invalidation maximizes hit ratio (>95%) and shields the origin during traffic surges.
tradeOffs.con: Requires reliable purge orchestration in your CMS/backend; a missed purge webhook leaves stale pricing or broken UI live until TTL expiry.

tradeOffs.factor: Edge Compute (Workers / Compute@Edge) vs. Origin Rendering
tradeOffs.pro: Running A/B tests, JWT auth, and HTML fragment stitching at the edge avoids origin round trips and enables personalized responses from cached templates.
tradeOffs.con: Edge isolates have tight CPU/memory limits (e.g., 10–50 ms CPU time, 128 MB RAM) and cannot easily maintain persistent TCP connection pools to origin databases.

tradeOffs.factor: Multi-CDN Routing vs. Single CDN Vendor
tradeOffs.pro: Protects against single-vendor global outages (e.g., BGP misconfigurations) and allows regional cost/latency optimization.
tradeOffs.con: Doubles operational complexity: VCL/Worker logic must be abstracted, cache-purge APIs diverge, and splitting traffic across two CDNs halves each CDN's cache warmth.

failureModes.name: Cache-Key Fragmentation
failureModes.description: Including `Cookie`, `Accept-Encoding` variations, `User-Agent`, or tracking parameters (`utm_*`, `gclid`) in the cache key creates millions of duplicate entries for the same object, collapsing hit rate and evicting hot items.
failureModes.mitigation: Normalize `Accept-Encoding` to `br`/`gzip`, strip all non-functional query parameters at the edge, and exclude cookies unless explicitly required for auth.

failureModes.name: Thundering Herd / Cache Stampede
failureModes.description: When a hot object expires or is purged, hundreds of concurrent requests at the same PoP see a miss and simultaneously hit the origin, causing a CPU/DB meltdown.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable request coalescing (collapsed forwarding) at both edge PoPs and Origin Shield, and serve stale responses via `stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error`.

failureModes.name: Private Data Leakage via Shared Cache
failureModes.description: Misconfiguring the CDN to ignore `Set-Cookie` or cache responses containing `Authorization` headers without `Cache-Control: private` serves User A's account page to User B.
failureModes.mitigation: Default to `Cache-Control: private, no-store` on all authenticated routes, strip `Set-Cookie` on cacheable responses, and enforce automated CI tests checking response headers.

failureModes.name: Origin-to-Edge Connection Exhaustion
failureModes.description: Without Origin Shielding or persistent HTTP/2 origin connections, 300+ edge PoPs opening fresh TLS connections to the origin exhaust origin TLS handshakes and file descriptors.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable Origin Shielding, use HTTP/2 or persistent keep-alive pools between shield and origin, and enforce mTLS or authenticated origin pulls (Cloudflare Origin CA) to block bypass traffic.

commonMistakes: Using `Cache-Control: no-cache` thinking it disables caching—it actually allows storing the response while forcing a conditional `If-None-Match` / `ETag` revalidation on every request (`no-store` is what forbids storage).
Purging the entire cache (`Purge Everything`) during deploys instead of using content-hashed filenames (`app.8f3a1c.js`) or targeted `Surrogate-Key` tags, triggering an immediate origin stampede.
Leaving the origin IP publicly reachable in DNS history or firewall rules, allowing attackers to bypass the CDN WAF and DDoS shield directly.
Caching 5xx or 404 error pages with long TTLs during a brief origin blip, prolonging a 5-second outage into a 30-minute user-facing failure.
Forgetting to forward `X-Forwarded-For` / `CF-Connecting-IP` or trusting them without validating the CDN's IP ranges, breaking rate limiting and geo-fencing.

sections.content:
## The idea

A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a globally distributed reverse-proxy tier that moves TLS termination, protocol optimization, and content caching to Points of Presence (PoPs) sitting at the network edge—often within 5–20 ms of end users.

Instead of every user traversing 15+ autonomous-system hops across oceans to reach a central origin, **BGP Anycast** announces the same IP prefix from hundreds of edge locations simultaneously. Routers naturally direct each user's packets to the topologically closest PoP, where HTTP/3 (QUIC) and TLS 1.3 0-RTT complete in minimal round trips. If the requested object is a cache hit, it returns immediately; if it is a miss, tiered **Origin Shielding** and **request coalescing** ensure the origin sees only a single consolidated fetch.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace what happens when a user in Bengaluru requests `https://shop.example.com/api/v1/catalog/shoes?utm_source=ig`:

1. **Anycast & Handshake (0–15 ms):** DNS resolves `shop.example.com` to an Anycast IP. BGP routes the user to the Bengaluru or Chennai PoP. Using QUIC (HTTP/3) + TLS 1.3, connection setup completes in 1 RTT (or 0 RTT on repeat visits).
2. **Edge Normalization & Cache-Key Construction:** Edge logic (Cloudflare Worker / Fastly VCL) strips `?utm_source=ig`, normalizes `Accept-Encoding` to `br`, and computes the canonical cache key `GET:shop.example.com:/api/v1/catalog/shoes:br`.
3. **Tier-1 Edge Lookup & SWR:** Suppose the edge PoP finds the entry expired 12 seconds ago, but the header specifies `Cache-Control: public, max-age=30, s-maxage=3600, stale-while-revalidate=300`. The PoP **immediately** returns the stale 200 OK payload to the user in 12 ms while firing an asynchronous background revalidation.
4. **Tier-2 Origin Shield & Collapsed Forwarding:** The background revalidation routes to a designated Origin Shield PoP (e.g., Mumbai `BOM`). If 40 other regional PoPs simultaneously missed the same key, the shield coalesces all 40 misses into **one** conditional `If-None-Match: "v42"` request over a warm HTTP/2 connection to the origin.
5. **Conditional Revalidation (`304 Not Modified`):** Origin checks the ETag, returns `304 Not Modified` (0-byte body), and the shield/edge refresh the TTL for another 3,600 seconds.

sections.content:
## Cache headers & invalidation mechanics

Mastering HTTP caching requires distinguishing between **browser**, **shared CDN**, and **revalidation** directives:

- **`Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=86400`:** Tells the user's browser to cache for 60 seconds, while the CDN holds the object for 24 hours. This gives you fast global invalidation without trapping stale assets in user browsers.
- **`stale-while-revalidate=300` & `stale-if-error=3600`:** The former hides origin latency during routine refreshes; the latter keeps your site online during an origin 502/504 outage by serving cached content for up to an hour.
- **`Surrogate-Control` vs. `Cache-Control`:** Fastly and Varnish honor `Surrogate-Control` exclusively at the CDN and strip it before sending to the browser, letting you set completely independent policies.
- **Tag-based purging (`Surrogate-Key` / `Cache-Tag`):** Tagging every product response with `product-123 category-shoes` lets your backend invalidate all affected pages in <150 ms via a single API call when inventory or price changes.

## Edge caching patterns & header reference

| Asset / Route Type | Recommended Header Policy | Cache Key Strategy | Invalidation Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Immutable Static Assets** (`app.9d2f.js`) | `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` | Path + normalized `Accept-Encoding` | Content hash in filename (never purge) |
| **Semi-Dynamic Catalog / CMS** | `public, max-age=30, s-maxage=86400, stale-while-revalidate=120` | Path + whitelisted query params (sort, page) | `Surrogate-Key` / `Cache-Tag` webhook |
| **Edge-Personalized HTML** | `private, no-store` to browser; `Surrogate-Control: max-age=3600` | Base template cached; Edge Worker injects user/geo | ESI or Edge Worker fragment stitching |
| **Authenticated User APIs** (`/me`, `/cart`) | `private, no-store` | Bypass cache completely | N/A (origin-served over Argo/warm tunnel) |

## Failure modes

- **Query-String Cache Busting:** An ad campaign appends unique click IDs (`?fbclid=xyz`), turning a 99% cache hit rate into 0% and flooding the origin.
- **Cookie Poisoning on Static Routes:** An analytics script sets a session cookie on the root domain, and default CDN rules bypass caching whenever a `Cookie` header is present.
- **Vary-Header Explosion:** Returning `Vary: *` or `Vary: User-Agent` creates thousands of cache variants per URL, evicting hot objects from PoP RAM.
- **Stale Error Caching:** Caching a transient 503 response because the origin omitted `Cache-Control: no-store` on error handlers.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Security & protocol optimization at the edge
sections.content:
## Security & protocol optimization at the edge

Modern CDNs double as your network perimeter and protocol accelerator:

- **Authenticated Origin Pulls (mTLS):** Configure your origin ALB/NGINX to reject all traffic that does not present the CDN's client certificate, closing the classic direct-to-IP DDoS bypass.
- **HTTP/3 (QUIC) + 0-RTT:** Eliminates TCP head-of-line blocking on lossy mobile networks (3G/4G), cutting P95 mobile page load times by 15–30%.
- **Brotli (`br`) Level 11 Pre-Compression:** Pre-compress static JS/CSS at build time with Brotli level 11 (15–20% smaller than gzip) and let the edge serve `Content-Encoding: br` directly.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Separate browser (`max-age`) and CDN (`s-maxage` / `Surrogate-Control`) TTLs, and add `stale-while-revalidate` + `stale-if-error` on all cacheable routes.
- [ ] Strip tracking query parameters (`utm_*`, `fbclid`, `gclid`) and unused cookies before cache-key computation.
- [ ] Enable Origin Shielding and request coalescing (collapsed forwarding) to prevent origin stampedes on cold PoPs or purges.
- [ ] Lock down the origin firewall/security group to accept traffic only from CDN IP ranges or mTLS Authenticated Origin Pulls.
- [ ] Verify that authenticated endpoints (`/api/me`, `/checkout`) strictly return `Cache-Control: private, no-store` in automated integration tests.

questions.title: Stale-While-Revalidate Directive
questions.prompt: What is the primary operational benefit of the 'stale-while-revalidate' Cache-Control directive?

options.text: It allows the CDN edge to return an expired cached response immediately to the user while fetching the updated version asynchronously in the background, shielding users from origin latency spikes.
options.explanation: Correct! stale-while-revalidate decouples user response time from cache miss latency, ensuring users always get sub-15ms edge hits while keeping data fresh.

options.text: It permanently disables origin server database queries.
options.explanation: Origin servers are still queried asynchronously in the background.

options.text: It forces the client's browser to store the asset on disk instead of memory.
options.explanation: Cache-Control governs expiration policy, not browser memory allocation.
Anycast is an IP routing mechanism independent of HTTP headers.
